transcript.content: Hello, thank you for coming in. Can you tell me what’s been bringing you here today?

Hi, yes, thank you for seeing me. Um, honestly, what finally pushed me to come in is... well, my shoulders and my neck just stay completely clenched all day long. It's like I'm bracing for a classroom observation that never ends. And the administration actually has been doing more of those lately, just dropping in unannounced. I teach preschool, so it's already pretty chaotic on a good day. Just last week, I had a kid manage to glue his shoe to the reading rug. I have a graduate degree, and let me tell you, they do not teach you how to un-glue a light-up sneaker from industrial carpeting in grad school. It took me twenty minutes and a lot of soapy water to get him unstuck. 

But, um, what was I saying? Right, the tension. It just doesn't stop, even when I go home. By the time evening rolls around, my jaw aches so badly I can hardly even enjoy playing my guitar. Which really bothers me, because I have this beautiful old acoustic I bought back in my twenties when I thought I was going to be a real musician. I usually try to play a little folk music to unwind, but lately my jaw is just throbbing too much to even focus on the chords.

Do you find yourself feeling anxious or worried about things other than work, like your relationships, health, or everyday events, even when there isn’t a specific stressor like an observation happening?

Yeah, it's... it's really everything. It's not just the classroom observations. My mind just keeps circling. Like, I start worrying about whether I'll ever get hired again if I lose this job, or if I've already ruined my reputation with the parents. Which, speaking of parents, I had this one mom last year who brought in these homemade, gluten-free, dairy-free, sugar-free muffins for her kid's birthday, and they were essentially just baked sawdust. The kids wouldn't touch them, and I had to spend an hour trying to convince a room full of four-year-olds that they were "magic energy cakes." It was exhausting. 

But anyway, yeah, the worry. I worry about whether retirement is just slipping away from me entirely. And then I'll find myself panicking over the smallest things, like if I make a tiny mistake during a story-time activity, suddenly I'm convinced it means I shouldn't even be trusted with children anymore. It's just this constant loop in my head.

When you're feeling particularly stressed or anxious, do you notice any other physical symptoms besides the tension in your neck, shoulders, and jaw—like stomach issues, headaches, or trouble sleeping?

Well, sleep is... yeah, sleep is a real problem. Most nights I just lie there in the dark, and my brain is like a television that's stuck on the worst channel. I'm replaying things I said in job interviews from five years ago, or I'm mentally tallying up bills, or trying to remember if I filled out the state licensing forms right. Which, by the way, those forms are a nightmare now. They changed the entire portal system in January, and it's supposed to be "streamlined," but you need a password that has a capital letter, a number, a symbol, and probably a drop of blood just to log in. I got locked out three times last month because I couldn't remember which special character I used. I had to call the IT help desk, and the guy on the phone sounded like he was about twelve years old and completely over it. 

But, um, anyway, the sleep thing. Even when I finally do manage to drift off, it's not restful. I almost always wake up around four in the morning, and my body is already completely tense. Like, my jaw is already clenched again, and my mind is just immediately calculating everything that could possibly go wrong that day. So yeah, trouble sleeping is definitely a big part of it.
Do you feel that your physical symptoms, like the tension in your neck and jaw, are more severe or concerning than what others might expect in your situation?

Well, I don't really know what other people expect, to be honest. I mean, my jaw hurts so much sometimes I feel like my teeth are going to crack. But maybe other teachers feel this way too? I don't know, they never talk about it. Usually in the breakroom, the conversation is all about the laminator. Our laminator is from the actual Stone Age, I swear. It jams if you even look at it wrong, and last Tuesday it ate three of my vocabulary posters. I spent my entire lunch period trying to pull melted plastic out of the rollers with a pair of tweezers I found in the first aid kit. And of course, the principal walked in right when I was elbow-deep in it, looking like a complete maniac. She just sighed and walked back out. 

But, uh, what were you asking? Oh, if my symptoms are worse than they should be? I really couldn't say. I just know it hurts.
Do you find that your anxiety is constant throughout the day, even when there aren’t specific stressors happening at that moment?

Yeah, it really is constant. Even if the classroom is perfectly quiet—which is rare, obviously—my brain is just going and going. I try telling myself to just stop, you know? Like, I'll try to make a list, or maybe pray, or I'll go outside to weed the garden to get my mind off it. 

Which, my garden is a complete disaster right now, by the way. I planted these heirloom tomatoes back in May, and I swear the squirrels in my neighborhood have formed some kind of organized crime syndicate. They wait until the tomato is exactly one day away from being perfectly ripe, and then they take exactly one bite out of it and leave it sitting on the fence post. Just to mock me. I tried putting up this netting I bought online, but the shipping got delayed, and when it finally got here, it was basically just cheap fishing line. I spent two hours untangling it on my patio while my neighbor's dog barked at me through the chain-link fence. That dog never stops barking, I don't know how they sleep. 

But, um... right, what was I saying? The anxiety. So I'll go out there to weed, trying to just focus on the next practical step, just looking for some peace. But it doesn't work. One worry just hands off to another, like a relay race in my head, and before I know it, I've lost half the afternoon to it. Just standing there holding a trowel, completely consumed by dread over nothing happening at all.
Do you find yourself worrying about a number of different things most days, even when there isn’t a clear reason to be concerned about them?

Oh, absolutely. It’s just... it never stops. My mind keeps circling from whether I'll ever get hired again for the next school year, to whether I've already completely ruined my reputation with the parents. 

Which, the parents these days, I don't even know. There's this one dad who emails me at eleven o'clock at night about the snack rotation. Who is thinking about graham crackers at eleven PM? And his email signature has this massive, high-resolution quote from Steve Jobs that takes up half the screen, and it completely freezes up my phone every time I open it. I really need a new phone, honestly. The battery on this one just dies if the wind blows too hard. I was waiting for the bus on Tuesday and it just shut off at forty percent. I had to go into a CVS and buy one of those cheap portable chargers for twenty-five dollars, and the cable was so short I had to hold the battery pack up to my ear like a walkie-talkie just to check my messages. 

But, sorry, I'm getting off track again. What were we... right, the worrying. Yeah, it just spirals. I'll be thinking about my phone, and then suddenly I'm panicking about whether retirement is completely slipping away from me because I had to spend twenty-five dollars on a charger. Or I'll obsess over the tiniest things at work. Like, I made a small mistake in a story-time activity the other day—I accidentally skipped two pages in the book—and my brain just immediately goes to, "Well, that's it, you're losing it, you shouldn't even be trusted with children anymore." It just takes something so small and turns it into this massive reason why my life is falling apart. So, yeah, I worry about pretty much everything.
Do you find it especially hard to control your worrying, even when you try to stop or distract yourself?

I think I mentioned this earlier, but yeah, it's basically impossible to control. I really do try to stop it. I'll tell myself, "Okay, just make a list," or I'll try to pray, or I'll go out to weed the garden. 

Oh, speaking of the garden, I finally saw the squirrel that's been ruining my tomatoes. He’s missing half his tail! It looks like a little bottle brush that got caught in a vacuum cleaner. He was just sitting up on the fence, eating a peanut, staring right at me. Where did he even get a peanut? Nobody around here grows peanuts. Although, my neighbor across the street, Mr. Henderson, he does put out those giant bags of birdseed. The ones you get at Costco. Have you seen the size of the bags at Costco lately? You practically need a forklift to get them into your trunk. I tried to buy a bag of dog food there once for my sister's golden retriever when I was house-sitting, and I pulled something in my shoulder just trying to get it into the cart. I had to smell like Icy Hot for a week. The kids in my class kept asking why I smelled like minty medicine. One little girl told me I smelled like her grandpa's feet, which, you know, kids just have no filter.

But, um... wait, what was I talking about? Oh, right, trying to stop the worry. Yeah, I'll go out to the garden to weed, just trying to focus on the next practical step, you know? Pull this weed, move this dirt. Just trying to find some peace. But it doesn't work at all. It's like my brain doesn't even care what my hands are doing. One worry just hands off to another, like... like a relay race. And before I know it, I've lost half the afternoon just standing there holding a trowel, completely stressed out. So no, I really can't control it.
